# Preface {.unnumbered}

Bass players often know more than they can easily explain. A line can live under the fingers for years before its internal logic becomes explicit. This book gives those decisions a compact mental model:

> **Role → Motion → Groove → Interaction → Design**

## Why piano notation?

A bass note means something because of what surrounds it. C can ground C major, turn A minor into an inversion, hold steady beneath changing chords, or complete a rhythm begun above. An isolated bass staff hides too much of that evidence.

Every canonical example therefore uses two staves. The lower staff is the bass line: monophonic, practical in register, and playable on electric or acoustic bass after octave adjustment where necessary. The upper staff is context: harmony, metric reference, phrase shape, call and response, or controlled contrast. It is never decorative filler.

This is not a piano-technique book. Pianists may play both staves, bassists may isolate the lower one, two musicians may divide them, and producers may hear them as independent arrangement layers. The grand staff is simply the clearest place to see cause and effect together.

## How to use an example

1. Read the listening question before the terminology.
2. Hear the full texture.
3. Isolate **Bass only** and **Harmony only**.
4. For A/B examples, confirm that only one meaningful variable changes.
5. Compare the full texture with each staff in isolation.
6. Play the exercise, make the constrained variation, then hear the longer study.

Current-note highlighting links the sounding event to the score. A textual description remains available when audio cannot initialize. ABC source is implementation material and stays out of the explanatory flow.

Chord symbols are visual labels only. Playback sounds exactly the notes written on the two staves: **Full** plays both, **Bass only** plays the lower staff, and **Harmony only** plays the upper staff.

## What the page can and cannot say

Conventional notation can show metric placement, subdivision, pitch, duration, rest, accent, articulation, and register. It cannot fully specify microtiming, touch, physical attack, interaction with a drummer, or the stability of a performed pocket. When the book discusses those qualities, it names them as performance—not as properties proved by an eighth note printed early or late.

## The learning rhythm

Every finished chapter asks one question and introduces one idea. A two- to four-bar **Microscope** controls the evidence. An eight- to sixteen-bar **Music** study proves that the idea produces something worth practising. Between them, a small exercise and one constrained variation turn recognition into design.
